claims.text: The selected high-entropy alloy is uncharacterized for superconductivity in its starting state.
The emergence of superconductivity is governed by the alloy's electronic structure.
Formation of a superconducting gap governs the emergence of superconductivity.
The superconducting gap can be directly observed through in situ magnetic-susceptibility or electrical-transport measurements.
Magnetic-susceptibility or transport measurements at low temperature can test the proposed superconducting behavior.
The relevant low-temperature test regime is below 10 K.
Formation of a superconducting gap leads to superconductivity.
Superconductivity will produce at least a 20% decrease in magnetic susceptibility or electrical resistivity relative to the starting state.
A decrease of at least 20% in magnetic susceptibility or electrical resistivity indicates the emergence of superconductivity.
Superconducting behavior is expected to disappear above 10 K.
The exact temperature dependence of the superconducting gap is unknown.
The influence of alloy composition on the emergence of superconductivity is unknown.
Failure of either magnetic susceptibility or electrical resistivity to decrease by at least 20% below 10 K falsifies the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says that the superconducting gap will be directly observed, but the proposed measurements are only magnetic susceptibility and electrical resistivity, which provide indirect evidence of superconductivity rather than a direct measurement of the gap.

The predicted outcome requires a 20% decrease in susceptibility or resistivity, whereas the falsification rule rejects the hypothesis if either measurement fails to decrease by 20%. The prediction is satisfied by one signal, but the falsification rule effectively requires both.
The boundary confidently places disappearance of superconductivity above 10 K while the uncertainty field states that the exact temperature dependence is unknown.
